extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, scientists, and educated general readers interested in human evolution and sexual selection
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarises the evaluative principles and evidential standards Darwin uses to explain human physical, intellectual, and moral traits via natural and sexual selection. Focuses on criteria for attributing traits to sexual selection, natural selection, inheritance, and other causal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection as explanation for secondary sexual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence or modification of certain bodily characters (e.g. hairlessness of the female body, development of beards, coloured or denuded surfaces) can be accounted for by sexual selection: traits that affect attractiveness and mating success become exaggerated because the more attractive individuals leave more offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and analogies are given from Quadrumana and birds (naked facial surfaces, brightly-coloured skin, divested head/neck feathers) to illustrate how sexual selection produces ornaments or denuded surfaces; Darwin notes that sexual selection may act differently in the two sexes and may be manifested in size, colour, hair, voice, etc. He warns that evidence is sometimes scanty and that sexual selection is one of several possible causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female mate preference shapes tribal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Steady preferences by women for particular traits in men would, over generations, alter the character of the tribe by favouring men who are both attractive (by local standards) and able to defend and support a family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If selection operates on both sexes (mutual preference), the effect is stronger. Darwin uses ethnographic anecdotes (women able to select husbands among 'savages') to support the plausibility of female-driven selection affecting population traits and reproductive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of body hair likely a secondary sexual character
rubrics_metrics.description: The general hairlessness of the human body (relative to other mammals) is plausibly a secondary sexual character acquired by sexual selection, not an advantage selected directly for climate or function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes foetal lanugo and rudimentary hairs, comparative examples where skin denudation exposes colour (mandrill, rhesus), greater hairlessness of women across races, and cultural aesthetic preferences; Darwin contrasts this with the inadequacy of direct climatic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beard development via sexual selection and differential inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Beards were likely acquired as an ornament by males and transmitted mainly to male offspring, analogous to bearded conditions in some Quadrumana where beards differ by sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support comes from comparative anatomy (foetal facial hair in both sexes indicates ancestral bearded condition), distribution of beards across races, variability indicating reversion, and cultural practices of shaving or praising beards that may reinforce selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head hair length as an ornamental trait subject to selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Long hair on the head is treated as a late-acquired ornamental character that has been admired and selected for (e.g. literary and cultural praise of long tresses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites literary praise (St. Paul) and social examples (North American chiefs chosen for hair length), and notes inter-racial variability (negro hair vs. European tresses vs. American natives) consistent with late acquisition by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin colour may be modified by sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Although direct evidence is limited, the colour of the skin is plausibly affected by sexual selection because skin tint is an important element of beauty within races and analogous colour differences in mammals and monkeys are sexually selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin admits evidence is scant but points to racial preferences and mammalian patterns (males often darker); he uses analogies from monkeys (Pithecia satanas) and the developmental order (infants less different in colour than adults) to suggest later acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection and the inherited effects of habit explain greater male intellectual vigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater intellectual vigour and inventive power in men is probably due to natural selection combined with inherited effects of habitual activities, since more able men would better defend and provide for themselves and offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin situates mental faculties among characters subject to variation and inheritance; he treats intellect as selected for usefulness (e.g. tool use, language) and amplified by social/behavioral inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral qualities originate from social instincts, sympathy, and reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation of moral faculties lies in social instincts (including family ties), the emotion of sympathy, and the capacity for reflection; conscience arises when reflective comparison of past impulses with enduring social instincts produces a sense of obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin describes the components: (1) social instincts and sympathy, (2) appreciation of approbation/disapprobation from others, and (3) vivid memory enabling reflection. He links strengthening of sympathies through habit, example, instruction, and suggests moral sentiments could be partly inherited after long practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as product of social instincts plus cognitive development
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral being reflects on past actions and motives and judges them relative to social instincts; conscience is produced when enduring social impulses outweigh transient desires upon reflective comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives the example of a pointer dog to illustrate the mechanism (if it could reflect it would judge past behaviour), and argues that imagination and memory intensify conscience, implying education of intellect enhances moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in spiritual agencies arises from imagination and intellectual advance, not innate design
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs in pervading spiritual agencies and even in a beneficent Creator are not innate instincts but arise from the advance of reason and powers of imagination, curiosity and wonder; primitive beliefs are not reliable guides to innate truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes universality of belief in spiritual agencies but argues they follow intellectual development; he warns against using assumed innate belief as proof of divine existence, as it would imply belief in many malevolent spirits as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary evidential criteria for human descent from lower forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusive grounds for man's descent include embryological similarity, close structural homologies, rudimentary organs, occasional reversions, mutual affinities, geographical distribution, and geological succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin asserts these converging lines of evidence are robust: embryological resemblance (embryo patterns), shared rudiments and reappearances of structures, and biogeographical and fossil patterns together make the descent hypothesis compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms and sources of variation relevant to evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation in man arises from the same general causes as in lower animals and follows similar laws of inheritance; natural selection acts on these variations (plus use/disuse, correlation of parts, direct environmental effects, and sexual selection) to effect change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin details contributions: struggle for existence, slight fluctuating differences sufficing for selection, inherited effects of long-continued use/disuse, correlation (one part changing with another), and occasional direct effects of conditions; he acknowledges complexity and partial unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible or non-adaptive structures may arise from organismal constitution or monstrosities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some structures that appear useless and cannot be accounted for by selection may be due to the internal constitution of organisms, occasional strong peculiarities (monstrosities), or causes not yet understood; experimental study of monstrosities may clarify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cautions that inability to explain a structure by selection does not refute evolution; he points to domesticated varieties showing unusual characters and to experimental embryology (e.g., Camille Dareste) as promising avenues to understand such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion and variability as expected outcomes in inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters long inherited are apt to reappear (reversion) and show great variability, especially in crossed or hybrid populations; this can explain racial differences in hairiness and other traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites examples: hairy idiots reverting to lower animal type, mixed-race susceptibility to reversion, and population studies showing variable hairiness; he treats reversion as a common facet of complex inheritance patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/artificial practices can influence trait prevalence and potentially inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-continued cultural habits (e.g., habitual removal of hair or other mutilations) may produce inherited effects or at least alter trait prevalence, and sexual/cultural preferences can reinforce such changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin mentions Dr. Brown-Séquard's experiments and Salvin's motmot feather example as evidence that habitual mutilation or behaviour can affect subsequent generations; he notes cultural practices (shaving, praising beards) influence selection pressures.
